summaries.example: Imagine you promise to help a classmate, even though you would rather play. Kant would ask whether your reason is that keeping promises is the right thing to do, not merely that you might get a reward. He also asks whether everyone could follow the same promise-breaking rule. If everyone made promises they did not mean, promises would stop being useful.
summaries.summary: Immanuel Kant argued that morality comes from a basic rule of reason called the Categorical Imperative. This rule tells us to act only on principles that everyone could follow and to respect the humanity of every person. For Kant, people are not valuable only because they are clever, happy, useful, or successful. They have worth because they are rational agents: they can think about reasons, choose goals, and guide themselves. A good will is firmly committed to doing what is right. Because people often have wants that pull them in different directions, doing one’s duty can require self-control. Kant called this freedom through self-guidance autonomy. He described several ways to understand the same moral law: make your rule suitable for everyone, treat humanity as an end, think of yourself and others as lawmakers in a moral community, and act as a member of a possible kingdom of ends. His theory also distinguishes moral rules from advice about reaching a chosen goal. Later parts of the philosophy discuss virtues, duties to ourselves and others, justice, helping people, and the difficult question of how moral respect applies to people with serious cognitive disabilities and to nonhuman animals. The entry also considers how Kantian ideas might guide human choices about artificial intelligence.
key_ideas: Kant thought morality is based on reason, not only on feelings, rewards, punishments, or results.
A good action has special moral worth when it is chosen because it is one’s duty.
We should choose rules that everyone could follow.
Every person has equal worth because people can think, choose, and guide their lives.
We may work with other people, but we must not treat them as mere tools.
Kant’s ideas also raise questions about disability, animals, and whether future artificial intelligence could be a moral person.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kant’s philosophy gives us a way to think about fairness and dignity. It reminds us to ask not only, “Will this help me?” but also, “Could everyone follow this rule?” and “Am I respecting people as persons?” These questions can help with promises, honesty, bullying, technology, school rules, and many other choices. The source also shows that philosophers continue to debate how Kant’s principles should apply in difficult cases.

important_terms.definition: A person’s choice to do what is morally right, even when another choice seems easier or more fun.
A moral requirement: something you ought to do, even when you do not feel like it.
Kant’s name for the basic moral command that applies to every rational person without exceptions based on personal wants.
Treating people as valuable in themselves, not merely as tools for getting what you want.
The ability to guide yourself by reasons and moral rules instead of simply being pushed by wishes or outside pressure.

questions_to_think_about: Is an action still good if someone does it only to get a prize?
What would happen if everyone followed the rule you are considering?
How can you use someone’s help while still respecting that person?
Does being free mean doing whatever you want, or can rules be part of freedom?

summaries.example: Suppose a student considers copying answers during an exam because the grade matters. The student’s maxim might be: “When cheating benefits me, I will present work as my own.” Kant’s universal-law test asks whether this policy could function if everyone followed it. If cheating were universal, the practice of assessment and the meaning of honest answers would be undermined, so the maxim appears to defeat the very practice it depends on. The humanity formulation adds that deceiving teachers and other students uses their rational agency merely as instruments rather than allowing them to respond knowingly.
summaries.summary: Kant’s moral philosophy seeks a supreme principle that explains why moral requirements have authority over rational agents. He calls this principle the Categorical Imperative. Unlike hypothetical imperatives, which depend on a chosen goal, the Categorical Imperative applies unconditionally. Kant develops several formulations. The universal-law formulation asks whether one’s maxim could be a law for everyone. The humanity formulation says that rational nature must always be treated as an end, never merely as a means. The autonomy formulation presents rational agents as authors of universal laws, while the kingdom-of-ends formulation imagines a moral community of equal lawmakers. Kant held that these formulations express one moral law, although commentators debate exactly how they are related.
key_ideas: Kant’s project begins by analyzing ordinary moral ideas such as good will, duty, and obligation, then seeks an a priori foundation for them.
Moral requirements are categorical: they do not depend on a person’s chosen goals, anticipated rewards, or likely outcomes.
The universal-law test evaluates a maxim first for whether it can be conceived as universal, and then for whether it can be rationally willed as universal.
The humanity formulation grounds equal respect for persons; it does not forbid all use of others as means, but forbids using them merely as means.
Kant links freedom with autonomy, but his argument from rational agency to the authority of the Categorical Imperative remains contested.
Readers disagree about whether Kant’s theory is strictly deontological or whether value, such as humanity or autonomy, helps explain why duties have authority.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kant offers a demanding account of equal dignity. His theory challenges decisions based only on convenience, preference, social pressure, or aggregate benefit. It makes intention and the principle behind an action morally important, while also recognizing duties concerning justice, honesty, self-development, aid to others, and character. Its difficulties are equally important: interpreters debate freedom and determinism, the role of consequences, the status of disabled people and animals, the place of emotion, and whether current AI systems could ever qualify as autonomous moral agents.

important_terms.definition: An unconditional principle of practical reason: it binds rational agents simply as rational agents, not because they happen to want a particular goal.
A personal policy for acting, usually specifying an action, circumstances, and an intended end; Kant evaluates maxims morally.
A conditional rational requirement: if an agent wills an end, the agent must will the necessary means to it.
Freedom understood as self-government: the rational will is author of the law that binds it, rather than being governed by external desires or authorities.
The requirement to value rational nature in oneself and others, never treating persons merely as tools for one’s purposes.
A community imagined as made up of rational agents who are equally bound by, and in a sense legislate, universal moral laws.
Moral strength: the stable capacity to fulfill duty despite contrary desires and pressures.

questions_to_think_about: Does the universalization test reject a maxim because it is logically impossible, because it cannot be rationally willed, or both?
Can an action motivated by sympathy have moral worth, or must duty be the decisive motive?
If a rule produces better consequences but cannot be willed as universal, what would Kant say?
Can a person be autonomous while acting under strong psychological or social pressures?
What should a Kantian framework imply for people or systems whose capacities for moral reasoning are uncertain?

summaries.example: A student group is deciding whether to spread a false rumor to win an election for class representative. Their rule might be: “When a lie helps our team win, we may use it.” Kant would ask what would happen if every group used that rule. Trust in statements would weaken, and the plan would depend on other people still believing words while the group secretly rejected honest communication. Kant would also ask whether the rumor treats classmates as people who can judge for themselves, or merely as objects to control.
summaries.summary: Kant’s moral philosophy asks what makes a moral rule binding on us. He argues that morality is grounded in practical reason, the kind of reasoning used to decide what to do. Its central principle is the Categorical Imperative, an unconditional command for rational agents. Kant gives several connected versions of it. One asks us to act only on maxims that could be universal laws. Another says to treat humanity in every person, including oneself, as an end and never merely as a means. Other versions focus on autonomy and membership in a possible kingdom of ends, where rational beings are equally governed by universal laws.
key_ideas: Kant says the deepest moral principle comes from rationality and applies without depending on what we happen to desire.
An action that matches a duty is not necessarily morally worthy; its moral worth depends especially on the principle and motivation behind it.
The universal-law test has two important forms of failure: a maxim may undermine its own possibility when universalized, or it may be possible but impossible to will rationally.
Respect for people does not mean never receiving help from them. It means not deceiving, coercing, or manipulating them as if they had no purposes of their own.
Kant connects morality with autonomy: a rational person is not merely obeying someone else’s law but governing the self through reason.
The entry describes continuing debates about disability, animals, consequences, moral realism, and the ethical responsibilities of people who design and use AI.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas give us tools for examining everyday choices and public rules. They encourage honesty, fair treatment, consent, and respect for people’s ability to make their own decisions. Kant’s view also explains why a good result may not excuse deception or coercion. At the same time, the source presents serious questions about whether Kant’s tests always give clear answers, how freedom fits with causal explanations of behavior, and whether his account gives adequate protection to people with profound cognitive disabilities or to nonhuman animals. important_terms.definition: The main moral rule Kant says reason gives to every rational person, no matter what that person wants.
A plan or policy a person uses when deciding how to act in a situation.
A rule that applies only if someone has chosen a particular goal, such as studying in order to pass a test.
Self-rule guided by reason; for Kant, freedom is not simply having no rules but helping author the moral rules that bind you.
The part of a person that can think, choose goals, and follow reasons. Kant says it must be respected as valuable in itself.
A moral community in which all rational members are equally subject to universal laws and are also understood as lawmakers.
The strength to keep doing one’s duty when desires, fear, or convenience pull in another direction.

questions_to_think_about: Is a lie wrong because of its likely harm, because of the rule behind it, or for both reasons?
Should an action done from friendship count as less moral than the same action done from duty?
What is the difference between using someone’s service fairly and treating that person merely as a means?
If everyone can make moral rules, how can those rules remain universal rather than personal?
How should human responsibility be handled when an AI system causes harm?
